2: Here's the rule the guide keeps.
The Security Operations book says it plainly: a dashboard is a picture of the evidence; what an assessor relies on is regenerating the numbers from the stored records.
The Compliance Automation book says the same of tests: one that reads a dashboard tile is a screenshot with a schedule.
So the workbook in this guide is a view.
Every tab says so, and the kit refuses to record a rendered view as evidence.
The evidence stays where it already lives: in the record each check writes, and the task each finding opens.
3: Workbooks are a flexible canvas over the most complete set of Azure data sources, and they can be managed as Resource Manager templates.
Portal dashboards give a single pane of glass, but a workbook is richer.
Dashboards with Grafana is a free preview; Azure Managed Grafana is for external sources and private networking; Power BI suits long-term trends.
Microsoft 365 has no single custom dashboard: each admin center has its own built-in views.
So the design is one workbook in the Sentinel workspace, and a link out where the data stays elsewhere.
6: Security operations is accountable for the sources, the template and the deployment, and for the telemetry tab each morning.
Identity engineering connects the Entra logs and the probe, and supplies the emergency access object I D's.
The endpoint platform owner connects Intune and supplies the compliance state value.
The operators read their own family's tabs.
And the security officer is consulted on each plan, approving its hash in the change record, and is accountable for the evidence.
11: Telemetry completeness comes first, because a dark source makes every tab over it unreliable.
Then each tab in turn: each row that needs work becomes, or is matched to, a task with an owner.
Entra Health and the I T S M queue are worked where they liv.
The workbook never closes a task, pages anyone, or proves a check happened.
Step 6 keeps the evidence: the kit records the validation, preflight, plan, deployment, reachability check and rollback plan, each hashed and chained.
A rendered view is never recorded.
And a portal edit comes back as an export, is validated, and replaces the template through review.
10: Saving a shared workbook needs the workbooks write permission, which Workbook Contributor grants, and deploying through Resource Manager also needs deployment rights.
Grant both on the workbook's resource group only, for the deployment window.
Readers need Workbook Reader and their own access to the data.
The test stage runs preflight, plans with what-if, deploys the approved plan, and checks reachability.
It's a go when each of those has a passing lyve record.
Production runs the same commands, and the preflight refuses it until the test stage's evidence passes.
Rolling back deletes a view only.
9: Step 2 fills one settings file per environment, and checks the two values the kit can't know: the compliance state your workspace records, and the product names of D L P alerts.
Those values, and every I D, go into the deployed workbook's parameters, never into the template.
Then the validator runs ten checks on the template, which matters because Microsoft says an exported template embeds sensitive values that should be masked.
Step 3 plans the deployment of one workbook resource and previews it with what-if, which changes nothing.
A second person approves the plan's hash, and the kit refuses any plan that would delete.
1: This is the narrated briefing for a companion guide in the Federal Modernization Workbook: The Daily Checks on One Dashboard.
One thing first: the guide has been reviewed and approved.
It answers a question the operator runbook leaves open: can the operator see all of the daily checks in one place each morning?
Mostly yes, on one Azure Monitor workbook in the Sentinel workspace, with a link out to the portal that holds the data for the checks a workbook can't read.
Its facts come from Microsoft Learn, read on November eighteenth and nineteenth, 2026.
We'll go in four parts: why, what, who, and how.
4: Here are the twelve tabs, one per daily check.

Telemetry completeness, the synchronization probe, risky users and sign-ins, and emergency access sign-ins fit strongly; the sync tab now also shows the synchronization servers' own errors and their nightly backup.
The new Active Directory tab, noncompliant devices and D L P alerts fit well.
Grants, the new admin changes tab and the log review queue are partial: matching each change to a ticket stays in the I T S M tool, and the review stays a recorded procedure.
Entra Health is a link-out, because its alerts aren't in Log Analytics.
And the catalog tasks liv in the I T S M tool's own dashboards.
Each server has its own row, so one that stops sending shows as stale, never as a quiet night.
5: What's available in G C C?
G C C Moderate uses the commercial Entra service and pairs with commercial Azure, so the workspace, the workbook and the Logs Ingestion A P I are all in commercial Azure.
Entra and Intune both send their logs to the workspace; Intune in G C C is the commercial instance.
Defender X D R alerts and incidents are generally available for G C C.
The Defender portal's connector overview is a commercial-cloud preview, so it isn't assumed.

For the servers that stay on premises, the Azure Monitor Agent on Arc-enabled servers, the Windows security events connector and the Azure activity connector are available in commercial Azure, and Defender for Identity alerts are generally available for G C C, with their own license.
And Entra Health monitoring and Connect Health, for sync and for A D D S, are not yet specified, so their tabs link out.
7: An Entra diagnostic setting sends sign-in, audit and risk logs to the workspace.
Intune's diagnostic settings send the compliance export, once a day, up to forty-eight hours late.
The Defender X D R connector brings incidents and alerts, including those it collects from Purview D L P. Health monitoring is turned on for Sentinel.
And the morning synchronization probe gets its own custom table, written through the Logs Ingestion A P I.
The check: a read-only reachability test reports each table as delivering, late or missing.
12: The workbook supports the monitoring the daily checks already do; it doesn't add a control.
Its records support configuration and change control for the template and the deployment, and continuous monitoring for the reachability check; the assessor decides.
The biggest dangers are a dashboard taken as evidence, and a missing connector that looks healthy.
The guards are the banner, the refused render, and stale shown as stale.
A silent server must never read as a quiet one, and the replication probe never runs from a lower tier.

Some things couldn't be verified on Microsoft Learn: the workbook's item format field by field, G C C for Entra Health and Connect Health, the synchronization service's event I D's, a right narrower than Enterprise Admins for the probe, and the values your own workspace records.
The developer workbook and the learning path take it from here.
8: Step 1 has three more sources, added for the servers that stay on premises.
The synchronization servers and domain controllers are Arc-enabled, and the Azure Monitor Agent sends their event logs and a heartbeat to the workspace.
That replaces any script that copies event logs to a file share.
The domain controllers' security events go through the Windows security events connector.
A replication probe sends one record per replication link to its own custom table.
And the subscription's activity log goes to the workspace, for the admin changes tab.

One right in the access request is Tier 0: reading replication forest-wide needs Enterprise Admins or equivalent, so the probe runs only on a Tier 0 host, and the Tier 0 owner decides whether it runs at all.
